"Alight" as an adjective means on fire or glowing with light. It describes something that is actively lit up — whether by real flames, by bright light, or even by a strong emotion radiating from within a person.

When something is "alight," it is burning — it has caught fire and is in an active state of burning.

  • The dry leaves were alight within seconds.
  • By the time help arrived, the entire roof was alight.

This is slightly different from simply saying something "caught fire." "Alight" describes the ongoing state of burning — the thing is currently burning, right now. A lit candle is alight. A burning haystack is alight.
Meaning 2: Glowing with light / Radiant with brightness

"Alight" can describe something that is brilliantly lit up and radiating light, even without actual fire. It suggests a vivid, active glow — not dim or ordinary light, but something that seems alive and shining.

  • The night sky was alight with a thousand stars.
  • The city was alight with fireworks on New Year's Eve.
  • The whole street was alight with lanterns during the festival.

Notice the key idea: this is not just "lit" or "bright" — "alight" carries a sense of something radiating light energetically, as if the light has a life of its own.

This is the most beautiful and expressive use of the word. When a person's face, eyes, or expression is described as "alight," it means they are so full of a strong positive emotion that it visibly shines through them — as if they are lit from within.

  • Her eyes were alight with excitement as she unwrapped the gift.
  • His face was alight with pride when his daughter walked across the stage.
  • The children's faces were alight with wonder at the fireworks.

Two things to notice here:

First, "alight" in this sense is almost always used for positive, energising emotions — joy, excitement, wonder, passion, love. You would not say someone's face was "alight with sadness" or "alight with boredom." The word carries warmth and energy.

Second, the emotion must be visibly radiating outward. You can't feel "alight" privately inside your chest. "Alight" describes what other people can see on your face or in your eyes — the way strong emotion shows itself outwardly, like a glow you cannot hide.
A critical grammar rule: "alight" never goes before a noun

This is one of the most important things to know about this word. "Alight" is what linguists call a predicative adjective — it must always appear after a linking verb (like is, was, looked, seemed, became), never directly before the noun it describes.

✅ Correct: The building was alight.
✅ Correct: Her face looked alight with joy.
✅ Correct: The sky seemed alight.

❌ Incorrect: the alight building
❌ Incorrect: her alight face

This pattern is shared by several English adjectives that begin with "a-" — words like asleep, alive, awake, afraid, ashamed, alone, afoot. You say "she was asleep" but never "the asleep woman." "Alight" follows the exact same rule.

You will very frequently see "alight" in the phrase "set (something) alight", which means to cause something to start burning — to put fire to it.

  • The arsonist set the warehouse alight.
  • A single spark can set dry timber alight.

This phrase works exactly like "set on fire" — they are interchangeable in meaning. "Set alight" is particularly common in British English.
The overall feel and tone of the word

"Alight" is not a neutral or flat word. It carries a sense of energy, vividness, and life. Whatever is described as "alight" is never dull or still — it is actively radiating something outward. Fire, light, or emotion — "alight" always suggests something that is alive and expressive.

This is why the word works so naturally for emotions. When you say someone's eyes are "alight with excitement," you are painting a picture of someone so full of feeling that it practically glows off of them. The word does something that a phrase like "she was very excited" cannot — it makes you see the emotion rather than just understand it intellectually.

The word also tends to carry a slightly elevated, literary quality. "The building was alight" sounds a little more vivid and dramatic than the plain "the building was on fire." Writers and journalists often choose "alight" precisely for this reason — it adds intensity without adding extra words.

• Ablaze — also means on fire or lit up, but usually suggests a larger, more intense fire or light than "alight." A city after bombing might be "ablaze"; a single candle is "alight," not "ablaze."
  • Aglow — very similar to "alight" in the light and emotion senses, but softer and gentler. "Aglow" feels warm and quiet; "alight" feels more vivid and active.
  • Illuminated — simply means lit up by a light source. It is neutral and descriptive, with no emotional energy. "Alight" always carries more intensity.
  • Radiant — when describing a person glowing with emotion, "radiant" is close in meaning, but it focuses on the beauty of the glow. "Alight" focuses on the energy and intensity of the emotion showing through.

"Alight" (adjective) means one of three things, all connected by the same core idea of something actively radiating outward:

  1. On fire — actually burning with flames (the cabin was alight)
  2. Glowing with light — brilliantly and actively lit up (the sky was alight with stars)
  3. Glowing with emotion — visibly radiating a strong positive feeling (her face was alight with joy)

Always used after a linking verb, never before the noun. Very commonly seen in the phrase "set alight." Carries a tone of vividness, energy, and active radiance in all its uses.
